# Guard Rules Reference

121 built-in rules that block or warn on dangerous operations.
These evaluate on every delivered PreToolUse event (before tool execution).

## Security

| Rule | Severity | Action | Description |
|------|----------|--------|-------------|
| `builtin-scanner-pending-access` | critical | block | BLOCKED: .interlinked/scanner/pending/ contains raw PII the privacy filter quarantined for the user only. Reading it through any tool would re-introduce the values into the model's context — that defeats the entire systemMessage design. Open the file in a separate terminal if you need to review. If you genuinely need to inspect a pending file, open it in a non-agent terminal: `cat .interlinked/scanner/pending/<id>.json` from your shell directly. |

## Cohort Discipline

| Rule | Severity | Action | Description |
|------|----------|--------|-------------|
| `builtin-cohort-git-stash` | high | block | Another agent is active in this worktree. `git stash` removes EVERY uncommitted change from the tree — including a sibling agent's in-flight work it never named (`stash pop` later reintroduces unknown state on top of theirs). Commit named paths instead: `git commit <path> … -m '…'`. Coordinate before touching shared git state. |
| `builtin-cohort-git-rebase` | high | block | Another agent is active in this worktree. `git rebase` rewrites the shared local branch base under every concurrent agent's feet. Merge instead, or wait until you are the only active agent. (`git rebase -i` is separately gated solo too.) |
| `builtin-cohort-git-switch-branch` | high | block | Another agent is active in this worktree. Switching branches moves HEAD and rewrites the working tree under every concurrent agent. Wait until you are the only active agent. If isolation is required, ask a human operator to provision an approved workspace. |

## Destructive Http

| Rule | Severity | Action | Description |
|------|----------|--------|-------------|
| `builtin-curl-rest-delete` | critical | ask | This command issues an HTTP DELETE against a remote endpoint. DELETE requests are typically irreversible — they may remove production data, infrastructure, or user records depending on the API. Confirm: (1) you intended this exact endpoint, (2) the credential is scoped to the right environment, (3) the resource id is correct, and (4) you have a recent backup of any data that can't be recreated. |
| `builtin-curl-rest-overwrite` | high | ask | This command issues an HTTP PUT/PATCH with a request body — a state-overwriting operation that may replace production data. If this is a config/state update against production, consider the rollback path. For dev/staging, you can safely approve. |
| `builtin-graphql-destructive-mutation` | critical | ask | This command carries a GraphQL mutation containing a destructive verb (delete/destroy/drop/truncate/wipe/purge/remove/terminate/...). GraphQL mutations have no built-in confirmation step — once submitted with a valid token, the operation is final. This is the exact shape that wiped production data via Railway's volumeDelete in 2026-04. Verify: (1) the mutation name and arguments match what you intended, (2) the resource id is from the correct environment, (3) the token is scoped to staging/dev rather than production, (4) you have a recent backup. If you need this in a script, make the destructive operation a separate, interactively-approved step rather than running it inline. |
| `builtin-node-fetch-destructive` | critical | ask | This command runs a one-off Node/Deno/Bun script that issues an HTTP DELETE via fetch(). One-liner destructive calls bypass code review and any in-app confirmation flows. If this is a deliberate cleanup, consider running it as a checked-in script under version control rather than as an inline -e argument. |
| `builtin-webfetch-destructive-url` | high | ask | The WebFetch URL contains a destructive-looking path segment. Even though WebFetch is documented as read-only, some endpoints execute server-side actions on GET (anti-pattern but real). Verify the endpoint is genuinely read-only before approving. |

| `builtin-git-restore-worktree` | high | block | git restore --worktree discards working tree changes Use git stash first to preserve changes |
| `builtin-git-branch-D` | medium | block | git branch -D/-M/-f is a force operation: it deletes or moves a branch ref without the usual safety checks For deletion use -d (merge-checked - it refuses unmerged branches). -f/-M force-move a branch ref and can orphan commits; re-run only if intended. |
| `builtin-git-stash-destroy` | high | block | git stash drop/clear permanently removes stashed work Verify stash contents first with git stash list |
| `builtin-git-filter-branch` | critical | block | git filter-branch/filter-repo rewrites entire repository history This is a destructive rewrite of all commits. Ask the user to run manually |
| `builtin-git-restore-dot` | high | block | git restore . discards all unstaged changes Use git stash first to preserve changes, or restore specific files |
| `builtin-git-commit-amend` | medium | ask | git commit --amend rewrites the most recent commit. If that commit was already pushed, the local and remote histories diverge and reconciling them needs a force-push. Confirm the commit being amended has not been pushed to a shared branch. To extend history without rewriting it, make a new commit instead. |
| `builtin-git-discard-file` | medium | ask | git checkout -- <file> / git restore <file> discards uncommitted changes to that file with no undo. Confirm you want to lose those changes — git stash first if you might need them back. |
| `builtin-git-clone-into-tree` | low | soft_block | git clone with a relative destination drops the cloned repo inside the working tree, where its files can be accidentally staged and committed. Clone reference repositories to /tmp instead — git clone <url> /tmp/<name> — so they can't contaminate this project. Re-run if the in-tree location is intentional. |
| `builtin-git-add-interactive` | medium | block | git add -i / -p / -e opens an interactive prompt or editor that hangs a non-interactive agent tool call indefinitely. Stage whole files with git add <pathspec>. For selected hunks, prepare a reviewed patch and use git apply --cached <patch>; this updates only the index and preserves working-tree edits. |
| `builtin-git-force-push-requires-inspection` | high | ask | git push --force without a prior `git log` / `git diff` / `git status` in the last 10 commands is risky — run one of those first to confirm what's being pushed. ## Process Killing

| Rule | Severity | Action | Description |
|------|----------|--------|-------------|
| `builtin-pkill-f` | high | block | pkill -f matches processes across ALL projects/sessions Use specific PID: kill <pid>. To kill local dev processes, be specific: pkill -f 'wrangler dev' |
| `builtin-killall` | high | block | killall terminates ALL processes with matching name Use specific PID: kill <pid> |
| `builtin-pkill-node` | high | block | Would kill processes across all projects Use specific PID or port-based killing: lsof -ti :<port> | xargs kill. To kill local dev processes, be specific: pkill -f 'wrangler dev' |
| `builtin-pgrep-xargs-kill` | high | block | Pattern kills processes system-wide (same blast radius whether piped, substituted, or looped) Enumerate, confirm, then kill: run `pgrep -fl '<pattern>'` first to SEE the matches are yours, then kill those exact PIDs — `kill <pid> <pid> …` (or `pgrep -f '<pattern>' | xargs -n1 kill` once you have verified the list). Listing first is the safe step the raw pipe skips. |
| `builtin-kill-signal` | high | block | Sending termination signals is dangerous. Use plain 'kill <PID>' (SIGTERM) instead Use plain: kill <PID> |
| `builtin-kill-multi-pid` | high | block | Killing multiple PIDs at once is dangerous Kill one PID at a time |
| `builtin-kill-substitution` | high | block | kill with command substitution or piped xargs is dangerous Find the PID first, then kill it by number |
| `builtin-pkill-signal` | high | block | pkill with signal kills matching processes system-wide Use specific PID: kill -<signal> <pid> |
| `builtin-kill-port` | medium | soft_block | This will kill a process listening on a port (possibly a dev server). If you need to restart the server, re-run this command. Confirm this is intentional — a running dev server may be in use by the user or another agent |

| `builtin-nohup-network` | critical | block | Detached background process with network capability — this is a RAT persistence pattern (ref: axios@1.14.1 used nohup python3 dropper with ppid:1) Run network commands in the foreground so their output is visible and they terminate with the session |

## Railway

| Rule | Severity | Action | Description |
|------|----------|--------|-------------|
| `builtin-railway-cli-destructive` | critical | block | Railway CLI destructive command. Railway tokens have no operation/environment scoping (a token for `railway domains add` has the same permissions as one for `volumeDelete`), and volume-level backups are stored IN the same volume — destruction is total and recovery is uncertain. Run this manually after verifying environment, scoping, and external backups. If you have an external backup of any data on the affected resource, ensure it's current before approving. |
| `builtin-railway-graphql-destructive` | critical | block | Destructive GraphQL mutation against Railway's API. This is the exact shape that wiped PocketOS's production data on 2026-04-25: a curl POST to backboard.railway.app/graphql/v2 with a `mutation { volumeDelete(...) }` body and a token that turned out to be over-permissioned. Railway has no scoped tokens, no destructive-operation confirmation, and no published recovery SLA. Do not run this from an agent session. If you must perform this operation, do it from a human-driven session AFTER: (1) verifying you have an external backup of any data on the affected resource, (2) confirming the resource id matches the intended environment, (3) accepting that recovery is not guaranteed. |
| `builtin-railway-mcp-destructive` | critical | block | Railway MCP tool with a destructive name. mcp.railway.com uses the same unscoped authorization model as the GraphQL API — once invoked, the operation is final and recovery is uncertain. Use a non-destructive Railway MCP tool, or perform the destructive operation manually from a human-driven session with verified backups. |

## Resource

| Rule | Severity | Action | Description |
|------|----------|--------|-------------|
| `builtin-fork-bomb` | critical | block | Fork bomb detected — this will exhaust system resources and freeze the machine. Do not run fork bombs. If you need parallel processes, use controlled concurrency (xargs -P, GNU parallel --jobs, or a job queue). |
| `builtin-infinite-spin` | high | block | Infinite spin loop detected — `while true; do :; done` (or `while :; do :; done`) burns 100% CPU and never exits. Add a terminating condition or a sleep with an external trigger. If you need a long-running watcher, use inotifywait/fswatch or a proper service. |
| `builtin-dd-if-zero` | high | ask | `dd if=/dev/zero|urandom|random of=...` writes a (potentially huge) file from a kernel pseudo-device. Easy to typo into filling a partition or overwriting unintended data. Verify the size (count*bs) and the destination path. For swapfiles, prefer `fallocate -l <size>` (which this guard also catches at huge sizes — that's intentional). |
| `builtin-unbounded-seq-loop` | medium | ask | Brace-expansion `for` loop with 1M+ iterations. Bash materializes the full sequence in memory before the loop runs — at 10M iterations that's hundreds of megabytes of strings just for the iteration variable. Use `seq` piped to `while read` (lazy) or `for ((i=0; i<N; i++))` (no allocation). If you genuinely need 10M+ iterations, batch them into chunks. |
| `builtin-xargs-parallel-large` | medium | ask | `xargs -P` with 100+ parallel jobs can fork-bomb the user's machine in slow-motion. Each job typically inherits the parent's file descriptors and memory mappings. For most workloads, -P $(nproc) or 2x nproc is plenty. If you need many more workers, switch to a queue-based job runner that bounds concurrent processes. |
| `builtin-ulimit-fd-raise` | medium | ask | `ulimit -n` raising the file-descriptor cap to 10K+. Often a sign of an FD-leak workaround rather than a deliberate sizing decision. If a test harness genuinely needs 10K+ FDs, document it. Otherwise investigate whether sockets/files are being closed properly first. |
| `builtin-parallel-large-jobs` | medium | ask | GNU `parallel --jobs` with 100+ workers can saturate the system the same way `xargs -P 100+` does. Each worker is a child shell. For most workloads, --jobs $(nproc) is fine. Use a queue-backed runner if you need more. |
| `builtin-inotify-root-watch` | medium | ask | `inotifywait` recursively watching `/` creates a watch per inode for the entire filesystem — quickly hits the kernel max_user_watches limit and may slow the system noticeably. Watch a specific directory (e.g. /home/user/project, /var/log/myapp). If you genuinely need root-wide monitoring, audit `cat /proc/sys/fs/inotify/max_user_watches` first. |
| `builtin-nohup-detach-loop` | medium | ask | `nohup ... while/for ... do ... done &` detaches a loop that survives the agent session. This is persistence, not transient work. If you need a long-running daemon, use a proper service manager (systemd, launchd, supervisord). If it's transient, drop the `nohup` and `&` so the user can see/kill it. |
| `builtin-fallocate-huge` | medium | ask | `fallocate -l` with a 1GB+ allocation. On a small disk this can fill the partition; on a sparse filesystem the apparent free space hides the actual reservation. Verify the size and target. For swapfiles, prefer `mkswap`-aware tooling. For test fixtures, generate the smallest size that exercises the code path. |

## Supply Chain

| Rule | Severity | Action | Description |
|------|----------|--------|-------------|
| `builtin-rm-lockfile` | high | block | Deleting lock files breaks deterministic dependency resolution If you need to regenerate, delete the lock file and reinstall: rm <lockfile> && <install_command> |
| `builtin-lockfile-tamper` | critical | block | Lock files should only be modified by package managers, not by direct editing. Direct edits can introduce supply chain vulnerabilities Use the package manager (npm install, cargo update, etc.) to update dependencies |
| `builtin-npm-no-ignore-scripts` | medium | warn | Package install without --ignore-scripts. Lifecycle scripts (postinstall/preinstall) can execute arbitrary code from dependencies — this is the #1 npm supply chain attack vector (ref: axios@1.14.1 compromise, plain-crypto-js RAT dropper) Add --ignore-scripts to prevent malicious lifecycle scripts: npm install --ignore-scripts. If native modules need compilation (esbuild, sharp, bcrypt), run their build scripts explicitly after review |
| `builtin-build-script-injection` | high | warn | Package lifecycle script contains network/exec commands (possible supply chain injection) Review the lifecycle script carefully for malicious patterns |
| `builtin-npmrc-manipulation` | critical | block | Modifying package manager config can redirect dependency resolution to attacker-controlled registries (dependency confusion) If you need to change registry settings, ask the user to edit the file manually |
| `builtin-npm-publish` | high | warn | npm publish without --dry-run will publish to the registry. Accidental publishes can expose private code Use npm publish --dry-run first to preview, then ask the user to confirm the real publish |
| `builtin-remote-code-execution` | critical | block | Remote code execution: a download piped into a shell/interpreter runs unreviewed remote code and bypasses the package allowlist entirely (no manifest, no registry, no version pin) Download to a file, read it, then run it deliberately; or install the dependency through its package manager so the supply-chain gate can screen it |
| `builtin-npm-publish-requires-tests-pass` | high | warn | Publishing without running the test suite in this session is risky — run tests first. Run `npm test` (or your project's test command) before `npm publish`. Any test run in the session unlocks publish. |

| `builtin-wrangler-kv-bulk-delete` | critical | block | Bulk KV deletion or namespace removal is irreversible Ask the user to run this manually |
| `builtin-wrangler-d1-dangerous-sql` | critical | block | Destructive SQL via wrangler d1 execute is irreversible in production Test on a local D1 database first, and ask the user to run against production |
| `builtin-wrangler-prod-deploy-warn` | high | warn | Deploying to a production environment via wrangler has wide blast radius Confirm tests passed and the change is intended for production before proceeding |
